name: Felix Gonzalez-Torres
bio: Felix Gonzalez-Torres (1957–1996) was born in Cuba and lived in New York from 1979. He was a member of the collective Group Material and made a body of work that uses the forms of Minimalism and Conceptual art to speak about love, loss and public life during the AIDS crisis. His works are often defined by instructions rather than objects: piles of wrapped sweets that visitors may take from and that are replenished; stacks of printed paper sheets to be carried away; strings of light bulbs; pairs of synchronised clocks; billboards of an empty, unmade bed. 'Untitled' (Portrait of Ross in L.A.) (1991) begins with 175 pounds of candy, the ideal body weight of his partner Ross Laycock, who died of AIDS-related illness in 1991. Gonzalez-Torres died in 1996; he represented the United States at the Venice Biennale posthumously in 2007.
studyNotes: One concept, many forms. Candy, paper, clocks, light bulbs, billboards and text all carry the same idea of a body that is present and diminishing.
The work is a set of instructions. Owners receive a certificate and guidelines; each installation can be different in size and shape, so the idea, not the object, is the artwork.
Participation completes it. Visitors take a sweet or a sheet; the work only means something when it is shared and slowly disappears.
Restraint carries emotion. The forms look cool and minimal, but titles and materials load them with love and grief. Look at what is left unsaid.
